nameStory: Euastrum pectinatum gets its name from its stunning symmetrical shape that resembles a tiny work of art. The word 'Euastrum' means 'beautiful star' in Greek, while 'pectinatum' refers to its comb-like projections that extend from its body like delicate teeth. This microscopic algae truly lives up to its name as one of nature's most elegant single-celled organisms.
description: Euastrum pectinatum is a single-celled freshwater algae that looks like a tiny green snowflake under a microscope. This microscopic organism is perfectly symmetrical, with two mirror-image halves connected at the center by a narrow bridge called an isthmus. Each cell is beautifully decorated with projections and indentations that give it an intricate, almost crystalline appearance. Individual cells are incredibly small, measuring only about 50-100 micrometers across - smaller than the width of a human hair.

idTips.label: Symmetrical star shape
idTips.description: Each cell has perfect bilateral symmetry with two identical halves that mirror each other exactly, connected by a narrow waist in the middle

idTips.label: Comb-like projections
idTips.description: The cell edges have distinctive tooth-like or comb-like extensions that give it a decorative, almost gear-wheel appearance

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: The cell appears emerald green due to chloroplasts (the parts that make food from sunlight) distributed throughout both halves

idTips.label: Central constriction
idTips.description: A clear narrow bridge or waist (called an isthmus) connects the two halves, often appearing almost pinched in the middle

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Invisible to the naked eye - you'll need at least 100x magnification to see the detailed structure clearly

habitat: Euastrum pectinatum lives in clean, acidic freshwater environments like pristine ponds, slow-moving streams, and bog pools throughout New England's forests and wetlands. It prefers nutrient-poor waters with low pH levels, often found alongside sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. Look for it in undisturbed woodland pools and the quiet edges of mountain ponds where water quality remains high.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. This is an excellent time to find them in temporary woodland pools filled by snowmelt.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when photosynthesis is most active. Cells may be actively dividing, creating beautiful chains of connected individuals.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Look in protected areas that maintain stable water levels.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist under ice in deeper water bodies, though they're less active and harder to find during the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being a single cell, Euastrum pectinatum is such a perfectionist that when it reproduces, it literally splits in half and then each half regrows its missing mirror image with mathematical precision - like a living, microscopic kaleidoscope that rebuilds itself!
confusionNotes: Euastrum species can be tricky to tell apart since they all share that distinctive symmetrical star shape. The key is looking at the specific pattern of projections and indentations - pectinatum has those characteristic comb-like teeth, while its relatives might have smoother edges, different numbers of lobes, or varied projection patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'algae,' Euastrum species are quite different from the slimy green algae most people know. These are desmids - a special group of single-celled organisms that are considered among the most beautiful microscopic life forms on Earth, often called 'the gems of the freshwater world' by microscopists.
compareHints: Euastrum pectinatum differs from its relatives by its distinctive comb-like projections along the cell margins. While species like E. bidentatum have just two main tooth-like projections, and E. oblongum is more elongated and smooth-edged, pectinatum shows multiple fine, regularly-spaced projections that create its characteristic serrated appearance. The overall cell shape is also more compact and star-like compared to some of the more elongated species in the genus.
